title: Uses of the Insanity Defense
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the insanity defense: its roots in ancient law and motive, the 16th-century English wild beast test, the M'Naghten (right-wrong) rule from the 1840s after Daniel M'Naghten shot Peel's secretary, the American Law Institute's irresistible impulse test, the 1984 Insanity Defense Reform Act after John Hinckley's acquittal, and shifting burden of proof. They cover historical cases including Richard Lawrence's attempt on Andrew Jackson, Ezra Pound's treason case, the Esposito "Mad Dog killers," Andrew Goldstein and the Kendra Webdale death (leading to Kendra's Law), John Delling's case in Idaho, which does not recognize the insanity defense, and Christopher Scarver's book plans. The episode ends with a long listener mail and mail-thanks segment and sign-off.
topics: Richard Lawrence Andrew Jackson assassination attempt

segments.title: Opening banter and chili talk
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about chili and lunch before introducing the topic of the insanity defense.

segments.title: Origins of law and motive
segments.summary: The hosts trace law back to Hammurabi-era ideas of motive and the distinction between accidental and intentional killing, leading to the premise of the insanity defense.

segments.title: Wild beast test and US variation
segments.summary: Early English wild beast test in the sixteenth century; insanity is not a medical diagnosis; US states define insanity differently with no single federal standard.

segments.title: M'Naghten case and right-wrong test
segments.summary: Daniel M'Naghten shot Robert Peel's secretary believing Peel was persecuting him; acquitted by reason of insanity and sent to Bedlam; the resulting M'Naghten rule (right-wrong test).

segments.title: American Law Institute and irresistible impulse
segments.summary: The American Law Institute's 1962 Model Penal Code test and the irresistible impulse / volition rule, with a Shawshank Redemption reference.

segments.title: John Hinckley and the 1984 reform
segments.summary: Hinckley's acquittal after shooting Reagan led to the Insanity Defense Reform Act of 1984, shifting the burden of proof to the defense and removing the volition rule; only a small share of cases succeed.

segments.title: Richard Lawrence and the attack on Andrew Jackson
segments.summary: In 1835 Richard Lawrence tried to shoot President Andrew Jackson with derringers that misfired; Jackson and Davy Crockett subdued him; he was acquitted and committed to an asylum.

segments.title: Ezra Pound's insanity plea
segments.summary: Ezra Pound, who broadcast pro-Mussolini anti-Semitic propaganda in World War Two, was charged with treason, found unfit to stand trial, and held at Saint Elizabeths, where he was later released in 1958.

segments.title: Esposito brothers Mad Dog killers
segments.summary: The Esposito brothers killed a office manager in a robbery and a police officer during a Fifth Avenue chase; their feigned insanity failed and they were sentenced to death.

segments.title: Andrew Goldstein and Kendra's Law
segments.summary: Andrew Goldstein pushed Kendra Webdale in front of a subway train during a psychotic episode; after multiple trials he pleaded guilty to manslaughter, and New York passed Kendra's Law.

segments.title: John Delling and Idaho's lack of insanity defense
segments.summary: John Delling shot three friends in 2007 while diagnosed with schizophrenia; Idaho does not recognize the insanity defense so he received life sentences. Hosts discuss a constitutional right to plead insanity and state repeals.

segments.title: Other cases and Christopher Scarver
segments.summary: Brief mention of Lorena Bobbitt's acquittal and Jeffrey Dahmer's failed insanity plea, then discussion of Christopher Scarver, who killed Dahmer and is writing a book.

segments.title: Sign-off and resources
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to HowStuffWorks articles on the insanity defense and sign off with contact information.
